task: This is a synthetic newspaper-writing exercise using fictional reporting notes. Use only the supplied reporting notes. Write from the reporting snapshot as of September 8, 2026. Write a headline and a 450–650-word AP-style reported feature about Threadword Services' changing translation work, focusing on the people, pricing and checking involved when clients arrive with machine-generated drafts.

facts.text: A July 2026 job note at Threadword Services records translator Aro Naylen comparing a client's draft visitor guide against an approved list of place names and opening hours.
The agency translates exhibition guides, booking messages and visitor information for museums and tour operators.
It has six employees and contracts with additional translators for language pairs outside the staff's coverage.
In the first half of 2026, 32 clients submitted machine-generated drafts for review, compared with nine in the preceding half-year.
Those figures count clients requesting that service, not every document handled or the quality of every machine draft.
The agency prices ordinary translation by the word but normally quotes draft review by the estimated checking time.
Review work can include confirming names, dates, omitted qualifications and consistency with earlier approved material.
A draft's existing length does not establish how much checking it needs or how quickly a translator can approve it.
Founder Anya Ravelle says some routine messages need limited revision while unfamiliar exhibition terminology can require specialist review.
Ravelle said, "The document arrives already written. That is not the same as arriving already finished."
Naylen says the agency sometimes asks a client to clarify the original source before deciding whether a draft translated it correctly.
Naylen said, "I cannot check a confident sentence against an opening time the client has not settled."
Threadword's client agreement requires approved source documents and does not authorize publishing every first draft without review.
The agency reports that paid review represented 28% of its first-half revenue, up from 11% in the preceding period.
The agency has not supplied total revenue, matched job complexity or staff-hour data sufficient to calculate a productivity gain.
No employee has been dismissed under the current workflow change, according to the owner, but future staffing has not been guaranteed.
Museum client Keri Varden says a single consistent version across signs, tickets and emails matters more than receiving the first draft earliest.
The reporting packet contains no machine-generated passages, outside system tests or universal error-rate comparison.
Threadword began in 2018 with two translators working above a stationery shop.
The agency is preparing a new client briefing on review scope but has not announced a uniform fee for all draft types.
